lesson.title: Lehnwörter II: Hotel, Taxi, Bus, Theater, das Hobby
lesson.subtitle: the travel-and-leisure layer — short Bus, long Theater, and the stress German imposes

hook.title: The Travel Layer
hook.content: The travel-and-leisure words are German's most cosmopolitan shelf — Latin, Greek, French and English itself, all pronounced with German rules. das Hotel is one word wearing three English masks: Latin hospitale became French hôtel, and English borrowed the family three times as hostel, hotel and hospital. das Taxi is a shortening: the meter on the roof that charged you was the Taxameter — Latin taxa, 'charge', the same root as English tax — and the cab took the meter's name. der Bus is Latin omnibus, 'for all' — a French omnibus car shortened until only the Latin ending survived. das Theater is Greek théatron, 'the viewing place' — and English theory is the same Greek viewing-root: a theory is a way of seeing. das Hobby is the newest arrival, borrowed straight from English and pluralized German-style: die Hobbys. And watch the stress German imposes: Bus is short and blunt, but Theater carries the beat in the middle — te-A-ter — where English says THI-ater.

footnotes.title: For All
footnotes.content: Omnibus is Latin 'for all' — the dative plural of omnis. The Paris passenger car of the 1820s was the voiture omnibus, the car-for-all, and the nickname outlived the joke: both languages kept the short form, bus, and forgot the Latin.

pattern.title: Taking the Bus, Taking a Taxi
pattern.content: Transport takes mit + dem: Wir fahren mit dem Bus in die Stadt. Destination takes zu or in + das: zum Hotel, ins Theater. The vehicle frame: Wir nehmen ein Taxi zum Hotel — nehmen does the taking. Der Bus kommt um sechs Uhr. Duration: Es dauert fünf Minuten mit dem Taxi. And the leisure frame: Mein Hobby ist Schwimmen — the verb dressed as a noun. The articles: das Hotel, das Taxi, das Theater, das Hobby — only der Bus is der, the one short blunt exception.
pattern.linguist_note: German stress is the arrival stamp. Bus kept its single blunt syllable; Theater moved the beat to the middle — te-A-ter — a Greek-French rhythm English never adopted; Hobby folded into German plurals (die Hobbys) while staying English in spelling.

exercises.prompt: The travel-and-leisure shelf in its frames — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: The bus comes at six o'clock
matching_pairs.german: Der Bus kommt um sechs Uhr

matching_pairs.english: We take a taxi to the hotel
matching_pairs.german: Wir nehmen ein Taxi zum Hotel

matching_pairs.english: We are going to the theater today

exercises.target_answer: Der Bus kommt um sechs Uhr, Wir nehmen ein Taxi zum Hotel, Wir gehen heute ins Theater, Das Hotel ist sehr teuer, Mein Hobby ist Schwimmen
exercises.explanation: nehmen takes the taxi, mit + dem takes the bus, ins Theater is the destination frame, and das Hobby dresses a verb as a noun. Five loans, one grammar.

exercises.prompt: '_____ Bus kommt um sechs Uhr' — which masculine article does the clipped vehicle noun Bus take?
exercises.meaning: der Bus — the one masculine on the travel shelf
exercises.explanation: Bus is the exception: das Hotel, das Taxi, das Theater, das Hobby — but der Bus. The shortest, bluntest word on the shelf is also the only one that refused the neuter default.

exercises.prompt: German 'das Schauspielhaus' or its Greek-rooted international twin names a stage playhouse. What is that English venue noun (US spelling)?
exercises.explanation: Theater is the same Greek viewing-word English kept: théatron, 'the viewing place'. ins Theater gehen — off to the viewing place. (das Kino, from lesson 5181, is where you watch films instead.)

exercises.prompt: Assemble the transport frame: 'We go by bus into the city'
exercises.target_answer: Wir fahren mit dem Bus in die Stadt
exercises.meaning: We go by bus into the city
exercises.explanation: Vehicle takes mit + dem; motion into a place takes in + accusative (in die Stadt), while standing in a place takes dative (in der Stadt, im Haus). zum in the bank belongs to destinations like zum Hotel, not to vehicles.

exercises.prompt: Say in German: "That's five minutes by taxi"
exercises.target_answer: Das sind fünf Minuten mit dem Taxi
exercises.explanation: Distance answers in time: das sind fünf Minuten mit dem Taxi. mit + dem names the vehicle, and the bank's zehn proves the frame scales — zehn Minuten mit dem Bus.
cues: Start with "Das" and anchor "sind" in position 2.

summary.outcome: Handle the travel words — der Bus, das Taxi, zum Hotel, ins Theater — and read the stress German imposes on its loans.

use_example.german: Wir nehmen ein Taxi zum Hotel — der Bus kommt um sechs Uhr.
use_example.english: We take a taxi to the hotel — the bus comes at six o'clock.

summary.takeaway: Hotel, Taxi, Bus, Theater, Hobby — hospitale, taxa, omnibus, théatron and English itself; Bus is short and blunt, Theater is te-A-ter, and das rules the shelf except der Bus.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: what you wear — der Schuh, die Hose, das Hemd, der Mantel, die Jacke.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Lehnwörter II: Hotel, Taxi, Bus, Theater, das Hobby (That's five minutes by taxi):
twist.target_answer: Das sind fünf Minuten mit dem Taxi
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Das sind fünf Minuten mit dem Taxi" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Lehnwörter II: Hotel, Taxi, Bus, Theater, das Hobby without relying on short-term echo.

hotel.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French hôtel — the same French loan as English hotel. [wiktionary]

taxi.context_phrase: Wir nehmen ein Taxi zum Hotel.
taxi.context_translation: We take a taxi to the hotel.
taxi.etymology_derivation: Borrowed from French taxi, the cab named for its taximeter — the identical French word English uses. [wiktionary]

bus.context_phrase: Der Bus kommt um acht Uhr.
bus.context_translation: The bus comes at eight o'clock.
bus.etymology_derivation: From Omnibus, the Latin for-all vehicle, shortened with influence from English bus — both languages took the same Latin dative. [wiktionary]

theater.context_translation: We are going to the theater today.
theater.etymology_derivation: From French théâtre, from Latin theātrum, from Greek theātron (a place for viewing) — the same viewing-place word English took as theater. [wiktionary]

hobby.etymology_derivation: An unadapted borrowing of English hobby — the same word, kept with German spelling and plural Hobbys. [wiktionary]

nehmen.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *nemaną — the twin of archaic English nim 'to take', surviving in nimble ('quick to grasp'); English take is a Norse import. [wiktionary]

fahren.context_translation: I am going / driving to Berlin.
fahren.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *faraną — the twin of English fare (farewell, bus fare, 'how did you fare?'). [wiktionary]

teuer.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *diurijaz — the true twin of English dear (d → t). [wiktionary]

stadt.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *stadiz — the twin of stead (homestead, instead); final d devoiced to [t]. [wiktionary]

fünf.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *fimf, PIE *pénkʷe — the twin of English five. [wiktionary]

sechs.context_translation: It is six o'clock in the morning.
sechs.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *sehs, PIE *swéḱs — the same root as English six. [wiktionary]

ärger.etymology_derivation: Back-formation from ärgern — from arg, bad; the verb page compares English eerie, from the same old Germanic bad-fearful root. [wiktionary]

fangen.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *fanhaną; the page lists English fang (to lay hold of) — the old catch-verb that survives in English as the tooth that catches. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
